en: Compiled by Dharma Master Yuan, Part 3: The Meaning of the Retribution of Suffering (Fourteen Sections). Within the Collection on Defiled Dharmas, the meaning of the retribution of suffering consists of fourteen sections: 1. The Meaning of the Two Kinds of Birth and Death; 2. The Meaning of the Four Modes of Birth; 3. The Meaning of the Three Existences (*bhava*); 4.

The Meaning of the Four Abodes of Consciousness; 5. The Meaning of the Five Nutriments; 6. The Meaning of the Five Aggregates (*skandha*); 7. The Meaning of the Six Realms; 8. The Meaning of the Seven Abodes of Consciousness; 9. The Meaning of the Eight Difficulties; 10. The Meaning of the Nine Abodes of Sentient Beings; 11. The Meaning of the Twelve Bases (*āyatana*); 12. The Meaning of the Eighteen Elements (*dhātu*).

Section 76: The Meaning of the Two Kinds of Birth and Death (Eight Original Texts). The Meaning of the Two Kinds of Birth and Death, explained through a sixfold classification: 1. Distinguishing the characteristics; 2. Classification according to stages;

3. Classification according to realms; 4. Classification according to causes and conditions; 5. Classification according to antidotes and abandonment; 6. First, the explanation of the names. [Sub-sections]: 13. The meaning of the thirteen [realms]; 25. The meaning of the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*); 14. The meaning of the forty abodes. **First: Explanation of the Names** 1. Distinguishing the Characteristics 2. Classification According to Stages 3. Classification According to Realms 4. Classification According to Causes and Conditions 5. Classification According to Antidotes and Abandonment **First: Explanation of the Names** [The text continues with the detailed explanation of the two kinds of birth and death.]
There are two kinds of birth and death.
This is from the Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra. What are their names?
First is birth-and-death by way of segments;
second is birth-and-death through transformation.
Regarding "segments":
The differentiation of the retributive fruits of the six realms across the three periods of time is termed "segmented" (fen-duan).
The initial arising of this segmented phenomenon is called "birth" (sheng).
Finally, one expresses thanks by saying "I am dead.
Regarding the term "transformation" (pariṇāma),
there are generally three explanations.
First, there is the subtle arising and ceasing of impermanence, which shifts and changes from moment to moment.
This transformation from what precedes to what follows is called *pariṇāma* (transformation);
this transformation is death.
This is called "death through transformation.
Therefore, in the *Bhūmivastu*,
it states that the suffering of birth, destruction, and change is termed "suffering of transformation."
This [power] is common to both ordinary beings and sages.
Second, through the illumination of conditions, one attains the dharma-body of untainted purity, whose spiritual transformations are unimpeded;
it is able to transform and alter.
Therefore it is called "transformation.
Transformation is death; thus it is termed "death through transformation."
This encompasses both the Great and the Small Vehicles.
Thirdly, because the true realized Dharmakāya is sovereign in its concealment and manifestation, and is able to transform and alter,
it is called "transformation and alteration" (pariṇāmika).
This transformation is not death;
it is simply that this Dharma-body has not yet undergone birth or extinction.
It remains subject to impermanence and the law of death;
as it undergoes transformation upon the body,
there is birth and death therein.
This is called "death through transformation" (pariṇāmi-maraṇa). It occurs only among the gods,
although it possesses three meanings.
What was spoken by Śrīmālā constitutes the second fundamental tenet; one should listen to these words within all the subsequent sections.
The death and rebirth in segments;
the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* also calls this the birth and death of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Śrīmālā is also called "unconditioned birth-and-death" (asaṃskṛta-saṃsāra);
this is likely a distinct name derived from the person [who taught it].
Ordinary worldlings frequently give rise to various outflow-tainted karmas (sāsrava-karma).
The accumulation of formations has a fruit,
which is called the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
This is the birth and death experienced by conditioned sentient beings.
This is termed "conditioned birth and death.
"Unconditioned birth and death" is established as its opposite.
Noble ones do not give rise to various outflowing karmas and thus do not undergo the retribution of fragmented existence.
It is called "unconditioned.
The birth and death belonging to the unconditioned sages is called "unconditioned birth and death."
The explanation of the names and meanings concludes this first section.
Next, the essential nature and characteristics are distinguished;
the segmentation of birth and death is indeterminate regarding its opening and closing.
In brief, there is only one;
or it may be divided into two:
first, the wholesome, and second, the unwholesome.
Humans and devas are called "good," while the three miserable realms are called "evil.
Alternatively, they may be divided into three categories.
This refers to all birth and death within the three realms;
it may also be divided into four types, namely:
birth from a womb, birth from an egg, birth from moisture, and miraculous birth.
This will be explained later.
Alternatively, it may be divided into five,
namely, the distinctions regarding rebirth within the five destinies.
Alternatively, it may be divided into six;
because the births and deaths within the retributions of the six realms differ from the aforementioned five.
Including the asuras, these are called the six realms;
when categorized according to their types,
they are infinite in number.
The divisions of the *paricchinna* (segmented) realm are thus; within the *pariṇāma* (transformative) realm as well,
the opening and closing [of these divisions] are not fixed.
In brief, there is only one;
or it may be divided into two:
first, the death and rebirth through transformation within the consciousness of phenomena (*dharma-vijñāna*).
Second, within the false consciousness, there is the death and rebirth of transformation;
among the six consciousnesses,
it refers to the retribution experienced by the object-perceiving and illuminating uncontaminated [wisdom].
The transformation and death within the consciousness of names and phenomena is called the transformation and death within the seventh consciousness;
that which is obtained as a fruit by taking the outflow-free (anāsrava) as its object is called the transformation and death within deluded consciousness.
Within that object-consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*), there is the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) in which cause and effect are distinct:
one performs karma in this life.
One receives retribution in future lives,
as explained in the treatise.
There exists a wondrous and pure land.
They have transcended the three realms;
such Arhats as these shall be born therein, and so forth.
Within that deluded consciousness, there is birth-and-death through transformation,
which is both coarse and subtle; that which occurs prior to the stages (bhūmi) is called coarse.
That which is on the ground is called "subtle.
Within that, the coarse aspects— namely,
the distinctions of cause, effect, and time— are similar to what was previously described.
As for that which is subtle:
the preceding thought serves as the cause,
and the subsequent thought manifests as the effect.
Within this, it is so subtle that it can no longer be discussed in terms of worldly distinctions;
it exists within every single thought-moment.
It is not problematic to further subdivide these distinct worlds.
Alternatively, they may be divided into three, namely:
the death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) of those belonging to the Three Vehicles.
Alternatively, they are divided into four,
as stated in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*: first, the arhat.
Second, pratyekabuddhas;
third, bodhisattvas of great power who are still prior to the stages (bhūmi).
Although they have not yet completely severed the two types of afflictions,
they are not dragged away by those afflictions;
furthermore, they possess mastery over taking birth within the three realms.
Therefore, he is named "Great Power.
A question is asked:
"Regarding the Bodhisattvas of Great Power prior to the stages (bhūmi):"
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that ordinary beings possess the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Why, then, does the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* speak of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*)?
The commentary explains:
In relation to the supramundane noble ones of the first bhūmi and above,
nirvāṇa is termed "ordinary person" (pṛthagjana),
for they have not yet severed the delusions of the two wheels belonging to the stages above the first bhūmi.
It is called "endowed with afflictions.
However, in relation to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others,
this is the purification of the two obstacles for these great sages.
Why can it not be said that there is transformation?
Therefore, it is stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
"The *srotāpanna* arrives after eighty thousand kalpas."
This continues until the pratyekabuddhas reach it after ten thousand kalpas;
that is, they reach the stage of "nature-attainment" (gotrabhūmi) of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Since these are already great sages, [they do not need further training].
What doubt can there be regarding transformation?
Regarding the four kinds of mind-born bodies (*manomayakāya*),
from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one takes birth according to one's will.
It is called the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*).
What is the meaning of "mind"?
Does it mean that it is produced according to the mind?
The mental faculty has three meanings:
first, it is swift;
second, it can reach everywhere.
Third, they are unimpeded.
From the first bhūmi upward, the assumption of a body is thus.
Alternatively, it may be divided into six.
As stated in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*,
these refer to the three stages and the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*).
Regarding these three stages:
This refers to the stages of the three vehicles prior to this ground: namely, those of the Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of great power.
Those three types refer to the three kinds of births on the first ground and above.
The three kinds of mind-made bodies are as described in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
The first is the body made of samādhi-mind,
which refers to those from the first bhūmi up to the fifth bhūmi.
Because the perfection of dhyāna is predominant, it is called the "mind-made body born of samādhi.
Second is the "mind-made body born of the realization of the self-nature of dharmas," which is achieved through the cultivation of wisdom in the sixth, seventh, and eighth stages.
To know that phenomena have intrinsic nature, and to know that phenomena lack intrinsic nature,
is called awakening to the self-nature of the Dharma-body.
The aforementioned intrinsic nature refers to the existence of a nature within phenomena;
it is the form (rūpa) within that which possesses phenomena.
The nature of being an obstruction is the nature of mind;
all such as these are termed "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, regarding what is called "nature":
These dharmas have no intrinsic nature.
Because they lack the true nature of all dharmas,
it is therefore called "nature."
Because it can skillfully illuminate both the nature of existence and non-existence,
it is called "awakening" (bodhi).
Third is the spontaneously born, effortless, mental body (manomaya-kāya).
This refers to the effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) on the nine stages,
which arises spontaneously;
it is called the "body of effortless action arising simultaneously with its type" (*jāti-sahaja-anabhisaṃskāra-kāya*).
These three and those three:
having already attained the full maturation of the karmic results of the nine stages,
they are of the same category as that which was cultivated during the preceding seven stages.
Upon reaching that stage,
when the maturation of the retribution manifests before one, it is called "arising together with its own kind.
Within the stream of the Dharma, it ascends spontaneously.
Setting aside their functional applications,
these three and those three combined make six;
individually, they are immeasurable.
The transformation is thus; these two gates are concluded.
Next, we shall discuss their positions according to a general and coarse classification.
Those who die through the breaking up of the aggregates are deluded sentient beings;
those who die through transformation are [the noble ones].
This refers to the mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) of Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of great power,
as well as ordinary beings and those in training within the Lesser Vehicle,
and the external ordinary beings in favorable rebirths within the Great Vehicle.
All [beings] within the three realms undergo birth through delusive craving;
this is termed "falsehood."
Among those of the Hīnayāna, they are the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas;
among those of the Mahāyāna, they are those from the stage of the spiritual lineage (gotra) upward.
By means of untainted karma and correct wisdom, they take birth.
Therefore, it is not deceptive;
that which is received through deception is called "death by fragmentation."
This is not a non-deceptive experience;
it is called "death through transformation.
Question: [Why is this so?]
From the stage of Srotāpanna upward in the Hinayana,
and from the ten stages of faith upward among humans in the Mahayana,
there likewise exists the merit of the fivefold Dharma-body.
Why is it not called "death through transformation" (pariṇāma-maraṇa),
but rather named "segmented death" (bheda-maraṇa)? To explain:
Because these persons within the three realms have not yet exhausted their birth through out-flowing karmic fetters and deeds,
it is called "segmented" [birth].
Although they possess the fivefold dharma-body of outflows-free purity,
because this is the causal dharma-body and not yet the fruition-retribution,
it cannot be called "death through transformation."
The coarse divisions are thus.
Within them, the subtle ones consist of two types of segmentation:
first, the evil destinies.
Second, the good paths.
The three miserable realms are called evil;
humans and devas are called good.
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna,
the [afflictions] of the evil realms and those of the stage of segmented existence are exhausted at the time of the Path of Seeing.
Therefore, the Srotāpanna is called "one who has paid off debts. This refers to having paid off the debts of the three miserable realms (*durgati*).
To further elaborate on this point:
At the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*),
the retributions of the three evil realms are all non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The karmic segments of the wholesome realms are exhausted at the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
Among those of the Mahāyāna, [this applies to] human beings.
There are three points at which the segmented continuity of the evil realms is exhausted:
first, karma of the evil paths acts as the cause;
second, the four abidings act as the condition.
The retribution of the evil realms is exhausted during the stage of the ten faiths,
because one transforms evil karma through practices such as the cultivation of the body or mental wisdom.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that they are reborn in the happy realms (*sugati*).
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* proclaims that the Bhadramukha can manifest as a Buddha.
Knowing this clearly,
one can also escape the retribution of the evil realms,
for which two types of evil karma serve as the cause.
The four abidings serve as conditions;
because the power of these conditions is weak and slight, they cannot pull forth rebirth.
Only by adding a small measure of compassion and vows does one accept a body in the evil destinies.
The stage of the lineage (gotra) comes to an end;
therefore, it is said in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*:
"A Bodhisattva of great power in the stage of the lineage is free from death by fragmentation (bheda-maraṇa)."
The three unwholesome karmas serve as the cause;
compassionate vows serve as the condition;
and the residual habits of the four abodes follow along and provide assistance.
Birth in the evil destinies is exhausted at the time of the first bhūmi;
it has not yet been severed prior to the bhūmis.
Because the first stage is exhausted,
the *Bhūmi-sūtra* proclaims that a bodhisattva of the first stage—
The *Bhūmivastu* proclaims that the Bodhisattva at the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryā*) is free from the fear of the miserable realms.
They transform the retribution of the evil destinies and enter the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, they accordingly assist in overcoming the afflictions of the four abodes (*catur-vihāra-kleśa*).
Because the first stage is exhausted,
the *Bhūmivastu* proclaims that the superior and middling afflictions of the miserable realms [are abandoned].
The first stage transcends [the preceding] because that which precedes the stage has not yet been abandoned or extinguished;
this is proclaimed in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Those of the lineage and those in the stage of practice may fall into the evil realms;
since the evil realms are thus, [how much more so for others].
The stages of the differentiated existence of the wholesome path also consist of three levels.
First, wholesome karma serves as the cause,
and the four abodes serve as the conditions.
Receiving the retribution of humans and devas,
when the period of their spiritual lineage has ended,
these two types of wholesome karma serve as the cause.
The four abidings serve as conditions;
because the power of these conditions is weak and slight, they cannot pull forth rebirth.
One must add a small measure of compassion and vows.
The bodies of humans and devas are exhausted upon reaching the first bhūmi;
prior to the bhūmis, they have not yet been severed.
Because the first stage is exhausted,
the *Laṅkāvatāra* proclaims that a bodhisattva of the first stage [is so designated].
One attains twenty-five samādhis and shatters the twenty-five states of existence (bhava).
Because these were not previously severed, they are proclaimed in the *Dharmapada-śāstra*.
Since even prior to the stages [of the path] there still exists the segmented birth-and-death (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*) within the three realms, that treatise states:
"As for what is called 'entering birth' up to 'attaining enlightenment in a single lifetime'..."
This refers to the realized wisdom of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
As for the statement "from eight births down to one birth," these are the births within the segmented existence (*prādeśika-janman*) of the three realms.
The three types of wholesome karma serve as the cause;
compassionate vows serve as the condition;
and the residual habitual tendencies of the four abodes follow along and provide assistance.
They are received at birth from one's parents;
they reach their cessation only upon attaining Buddhahood.
Prior to that, they have not been severed.
Because [the Buddha] has reached the ultimate exhaustion of all things,
the Sūtra praises him, saying:
"Only the Buddha has severed the seeds of the Peak of Existence."
From the tenth stage downward,
they take birth among humans and devas because they have not yet reached ultimate exhaustion.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* merely states:
"A Bodhisattva in the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryā*) transforms the retribution of the evil destinies and enters the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*)."
It is not said that they have turned toward goodness.
Furthermore, those from the tenth stage downward who take birth among humans or devas have not yet exhausted their afflictions.
Therefore, in the *Bhūmivastu* (The Foundation of the Stages),
it is stated only that in the first stage one transcends the afflictions of the miserable realms (*apāya*) within the context of surpassing [the lower stages];
it does not say that one transcends the afflictions of the happy realms (*sugati*).
Using these scriptural passages as evidence,
it is clear that the residual habits of humans and devas persist up to the tenth bhūmi;
within this, they are further distinguished.
The human *bhavāṅga* (segmented existence) is exhausted at the time of the eighth stage;
prior to that, it has not been severed.
Because the eighth stage is exhausted,
the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* declares that the eighth stage constitutes the state of an Anāgāmin.
One does not receive a physical body because what was previously [unwholesome] has not yet been severed;
this is stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The first seven stages are still characterized by the physical body;
as for the devas' limited lifespan, it is only at the stage of Buddhahood that it is completely exhausted.
Because they were not severed prior to that and only reach their end with the Buddha,
the Buddha alone has severed the seeds of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Because the [defilements] previously mentioned have not yet been severed,
those from the eighth stage upward are called only *anāgāmin* (non-returner), not *arhat*.
Question: Since all six realms of existence arise throughout the earth,
why do you specifically state that birth among humans and devas constitutes "segmented existence" (paricchinna-bhava)?
The commentary states:
Because their evil karma on the earth has been exhausted,
although they are born in the evil realms, [they do not suffer].
However, it is because the wholesome karma of humans and devas has not yet been exhausted that [the Buddha] manifests his presence.
They are born among humans and devas;
that which corresponds to their subtle karma from the time they were ordinary beings is called "segmented" (paricchinna).
Next, the transformational (nairmāṇika) [death] is explained.
Within the process of transformation and change,
there is cause and there is effect.
Among those of the Hīnayāna, [this is so].
That which arises from the cause of transformation occurs from the stage of the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) onwards;
that which constitutes the retribution of transformation arises after the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣaphala). What, then, is this?
As stated in the treatise:
there exists a wondrous and pure land that transcends the triple world.
One who is free from afflictions is an Arhat;
they shall be born therein.
Such are these categories.
Within those of the Mahāyāna, there are four stages of distinction:
first, the stage of the causal origin, which begins from the ten levels of faith (daśa-śraddhā) and above.
The second [type of death] pertains to those from the stage of the lineage (gotra) who have attained the fruit and above;
therefore, it is said in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*:
"From the stage of the lineage upward, great power constitutes the death of transformation."
Question: The *Dharmapada-upadeśa* states that prior to the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*),
one undergoes death by fragmentation (*pariccheda-maraṇa*).
Why did Śrīmālā say it is "transformation"?
The commentary explains:
above the bodhisattva lineage, there are five kinds of bodies.
First is the *dharmatā-kāya* (dharma-nature body),
which refers to the purity within the lineage of nature (*prakṛti-gotra*) and the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*).
This is as explained in the *Bhūmivastu* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
The six sense bases are preeminent and have been so from beginningless time as a matter of natural law; such is the case with these and others.
Second is the Body of Real Reward (*sambhogakāya*).

This refers to attaining the preliminary expedient means within the stage of the nature of the lineage through practice (*śikṣāgotra*) and the stage of practice and understanding (*adhimukticaryā*), as described in the *Bhūmivastu* (or *Yogācārabhūmi*).
It is that which has been attained through the cultivation of wholesome qualities from the past.
Such are these [categories].
Third is the dharmakāya of arising, ceasing, and transformation,
which refers to the fruit of outflow-free karma that is conditionally illuminated.
Fourth is the segmented body (*prādeśika-kāya*),
which refers to the fruits of contaminated karma (*sāsrava-karma*) from beginningless time.
Fifth is the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).
Manifesting in birth according to objects,
these five kinds of bodies each have their own causes and conditions.
Regarding the Dharma-nature body (dharmatā-kāya),
buddha-nature (buddhadhātu) serves as the cause,
while the realization of the [Dharma] gateway serves as the condition.
As for the true recompense body (sambhogakāya),
the six perfections serve as its cause,
and buddha-nature serves as its condition.
There is further meaning,
as explained in the latter two types of lineage (*gotra*).
Regarding the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*):
With untainted karma as the cause and ignorance as the condition,
there is the segmented body.
With outflowing karma as the cause and compassionate vows as the condition,
[they appear] within the Nirmāṇakāya and Saṃbhogakāya forms.
There are two kinds: first, the dharma-response (dharmānubhava), which arises based on the dharma-body (dharmakāya);
second, the retribution-response (vipākānubhava), which manifests based on the retribution-body (saṃbhogakāya).
These two types should each have distinct causes and conditions.
Regarding their doctrinal correspondence:
within the *tathāgatagarbha*, the transformative function of the *samādhi* dharma-gate serves as the cause.
Compassionate vows serve as the condition;
if one discusses retribution,
compassionate vows serve as the cause.
Taking the dharma-gate of the samādhi of transformative function as its condition,
among these five bodies,
the first two do not die.
Next, two will truly die;
finally, one should die.
Therefore, regarding those of the lineage and above:
Within the body of reality-recompense (sambhogakāya),
there is the admixture of transformation; within the bodies of response and manifestation (nirmāṇakāya and sāmbhogikakāya), [there is likewise].
There is a mixture of "segmented" [birth].
In the *Dharmapada-śāstra*,
it is explained as "segmented" based on the fourth category.
In the Śrīmālā-sūtra,
it is described as "transformation" based on the third category;
each [classification] represents a distinct meaning.
They are not mutually contradictory.
This is the second place for attaining the fruit.
Third is the place of gradual relinquishment.
From the first bhūmi upward,
the four limits of exhaustion reside in the stage of the Tathāgata.
The classification of the stages is thus concluded; these three gates are finished.
Next, we shall discuss them by way of the realms (*dhātu*).
"Realms" refers to the three realms.
Within this, there is a brief analysis by way of two gates.
First, the analysis according to characteristics:
birth-and-death in segments is subsumed within the three realms.
Because it is the fruit of contaminated karma within the three realms,
the death and rebirth of transformation is not subsumed under the three realms;
because it is the fruit of supramundane uncontaminated karma.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"There exists a wondrous and pure land that transcends the triple world;
this is the realm of the Arhat."
When one is born therein,
one clearly knows that the supramundane is thus.
All of them. Second, regarding the general discussion of their nature:
both types of birth-and-death are subsumed within the three realms.
What is the meaning of this?
As it is said in the Śrīmālā-sūtra:
"There are two kinds of worlds."
First, destruction by impermanence;
second, illness due to impermanence.
Regarding destruction by impermanence:
This is the three realms of the fragmented [birth-and-death],
which are characterized by impermanence and illness;
this is the three realms of the transformative [birth-and-death].
Birth-and-death by segments is still subsumed within the segmented triple world;
birth-and-death through transformation is still encompassed within the transformative triple world.
Question: While the boundaries of the *paricchinna* (segmented) birth-and-death within the three realms can be known,
at what point within the three realms do the boundaries of the *pariṇāma* (transformative) birth-and-death lie?
It is known only by the noble ones;
it can also be transformed,
as explained according to the stages of dhyāna.
Based on the stage of the first dhyāna, one gives rise to untainted karma (anāsrava-karma) and receives the retribution of transformation (pariṇāma-vipāka),
which is bound to the first dhyāna.
Thus concludes this section on the four gates.
Next, the causes and conditions are distinguished:
that which produces directly is called the cause (*hetu*), while that which assists indirectly is termed the condition (*pratyaya*).
In general terms, this is a rough discussion:
segmental birth and death have out-flowing karma as their cause.
The four abidings serve as conditions.
Thus, the Śrīmālādevī-sūtra says:
"Furthermore, it is like how the three realms of existence arise from the cause of tainted karma conditioned by grasping."
"Grasping" (upādāna) is equivalent to craving (tṛṣṇā).
At the time of taking birth,
one may give rise to sexual craving.
Alternatively, when attachment to lotus ponds and the like arises,
one immediately takes on a body; therefore, it is said that [craving] is the condition for receiving birth in the three realms.

therefore, at the time of death,
